Added Value of Preoperative Contrast Enhanced Mammography in Staging of Malignant Breast Lesions (PROCEM): A Randomized Controlled Trial

Gardfjell A, Rydén L, Niméus E et al. · 2026 Nov
Study Type: Prospective, two-centre randomised controlled trial (Sweden), n=415.
Key Question: Does adding preoperative contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) to standard imaging (mammography/tomosynthesis and US) change treatment or outcomes in early-stage breast cancer eligible for primary surgery?
Key Findings:
  • Primary endpoint not met: CEM changed treatment in 8.4% (17/202; 95% CI 5.3–13.1) against a prespecified 10% threshold.
  • No evidence of difference in mastectomy (17% vs 18%, P=.78) or reoperation rates (7.9% vs 10%, P=.39) between CEM and control.
  • CEM gave the closest agreement with histopathological extent (bias 3.5 mm vs 4.8 mm for mammography/tomosynthesis and 10.7 mm for US), better in nine of 10 subgroups; DCIS was the exception.
Clinical Relevance: For UK breast services considering CEM as an MRI alternative, it improves size estimation but did not translate into fewer mastectomies or reoperations, so routine preoperative use is not clearly supported.
Limitations: The trial was likely not powered to detect differences in mastectomy or reoperation rates, and the abstract does not report whether the 10% target was based on a justified clinical threshold.

Radiology

Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Part-Solid Lung Adenocarcinomas with a Maximum Solid Portion Diameter of 30.0 mm

Li X, Ma J, Chen W et al. · 2026 Nov
Study Type: Retrospective single-cohort diagnostic/prognostic study (n=1444), surgical series.
Key Question: Which CT features predict lymph node metastasis in part-solid lung adenocarcinomas with solid portion ≤30 mm?
Key Findings:
  • LN metastasis occurred in 4.7% (68/1444); none in 115 patients with CTR ≤0.25, and only 1/552 (0.2%) with solid portion ≤6 mm.
  • Solid portion diameter was the only independent predictor (OR 1.25 per unit, 95% CI 1.20–1.31) and outperformed CTR (AUC 0.86 vs 0.75, P<.001), with better calibration and net benefit.
  • A 7.3 mm solid portion cutoff gave 95.6% sensitivity but only 49.6% specificity.
Clinical Relevance: Supports risk-stratified radiological reporting of solid component size to inform surgical planning and the extent of nodal assessment in UK lung cancer MDTs.
Limitations: Retrospective, short-timeframe data (2023–2024) with no external validation reported, and the low event count limits model stability; applicability to non-East Asian populations is uncertain.

British Journal of Radiology

Cervicocerebral angiography in trauma using split-bolus whole-body CT - comparison with dedicated neuroradiological CT angiography

Shalamberidze G, Almeida GG, Damaskova O et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Retrospective single-centre matched cohort study (130 polytrauma split-bolus WBCT vs 130 dedicated head-and-neck CTA).
Key Question: Does split-bolus whole-body CT provide sufficient cervicocerebral arterial opacification and diagnostic evaluability compared with dedicated neuroradiological CTA in polytrauma?
Key Findings:
  • Dedicated CTA gave significantly higher attenuation in all segments except the cervical ICA (p = 0.08), but mean and median attenuation exceeded the 250 HU threshold in all 15 segments for both protocols.
  • Sub-threshold measurements (<250 HU) were more frequent with split-bolus WBCT, reaching significance only in the petrous ICA (p = 0.02).
  • Readers rated dedicated CTA higher for arterial contrast and lower venous contamination (both p < 0.01); diagnostic evaluability was high in both groups, with no significant difference for four of five readers.
Clinical Relevance: Supports using the trauma-pathway WBCT for initial cervicocerebral vascular screening in UK major trauma centres, potentially avoiding additional contrast and scan time.
Limitations: Retrospective design assessed image quality and evaluability only, with no reference standard (e.g., DSA) or analysis of diagnostic accuracy for injury detection.

British Journal of Radiology

A multi-reader multi-case study comparing Breast Cancer Reading Efficiency and Accuracy in Screening with Tomosynthesis versus AI-assisted mammography

Ning SGS, Hao D, Chandrasegan G et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Multi-reader, multi-case (MRMC) crossover reader study using a retrospective enriched dataset (Emory BrEast Imaging Dataset)
Key Question: Does AI-enhanced 2D mammography (DM+AI) match digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) for recalling interval breast cancers (IBCs) on screening images?
Key Findings:
  • IBC recall rates were similar (DM+AI 41.5% vs DBT 40.9%); detection rates were 14.8% vs 11.9%. SDC performance was also comparable.
  • DM+AI identified more non-invasive (31.5% vs 13.0%) and mass-forming (61.0% vs 21.8%) IBCs. By density, DM+AI recall was higher in fatty breasts (91.7% vs 50.0%), whereas DBT performed better in extremely dense breasts.
  • DM+AI reduced interpretation time by an average of 24.1 seconds per case.
Clinical Relevance: Findings support exploring density-stratified screening pathways, relevant to NHS Breast Screening Programme workload pressures and ongoing AI evaluation, although DBT is not currently used in routine UK screening.
Limitations: Small, enriched retrospective sample (106 cases, six readers) with no reported statistical testing or confidence intervals in the abstract, limiting generalisability and subgroup inference.

British Journal of Radiology

Comparative Study of Dual-energy X‑ray Absorptiometry versus Multislice Computed Tomography for Vertebral Height Measurement

Chan CH, Hsu AL, Vy VPT et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Retrospective comparative imaging study (single dataset of 34 patients with paired CT/DXA; second CT-only dataset of 114 patients).
Key Question: Do 2D midsagittal and 3D multi-slice CT approaches to vertebral height measurement yield different Genant fracture gradings, and how do these compare with DXA-based vertebral fracture assessment?
Key Findings:
  • Conventional CT grading (Method A) showed no significant difference from DXA (p = 0.33); the consensus (B) and global search (C) methods differed significantly (p < 0.001 each).
  • Reclassification was greatest for Grade 1 vertebrae (98 by Method B; 166 by Method C, of 191 vertebrae).
  • Methods B and C measured height loss 9–14 percentage points greater than Method A across Grades 0–2; the authors report an overall 3D–2D difference of 10.84 percentage points.
Clinical Relevance: Applying 2D Genant thresholds to CT may overestimate vertebral height loss, with implications for opportunistic fracture reporting and downstream osteoporosis referral pathways.
Limitations: Small paired sample (34 patients) with no clinical outcome or reference-standard validation, so it is unclear which method is more accurate.

British Journal of Radiology

Quantitative Hepatobiliary MRI for Early Prognostic Assessment After Liver Transplantation: Survival Prediction Using the Contrast Enhancement Index

Asmundo L, Mariani L, Mazzarelli C et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Retrospective single-cohort study (n=70)
Key Question: Can a quantitative contrast enhancement index (CEI) from Gd-BOPTA hepatobiliary-phase MRI within 6 months of liver transplantation predict post-transplant mortality?
Key Findings:
  • CEI was measurable in all patients. Non-survivors had lower median CEI than survivors (1.17 vs 1.31; p=0.03).
  • Discrimination was only moderate (AUC 0.667, 95% CI 0.529–0.793). At the 1.301 cutoff, sensitivity was 88% but specificity only 51.2%.
  • Lower CEI was associated with worse survival (log-rank p=0.028). After age adjustment, HR per 0.1-unit increase was 0.79 (95% CI 0.64–0.98).
Clinical Relevance: CEI is a feasible, non-invasive graft-function biomarker, but its poor specificity and the limited availability of Gd-BOPTA in UK practice currently limit routine use for post-transplant risk stratification.
Limitations: Small, retrospective, single-cohort sample with only age adjustment and no external validation. Cutoff was derived and tested in the same data, so performance is likely overestimated.

British Journal of Radiology

Assessing microvascular heterogeneity in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and peritumoral tissue using DCE-MRI pharmacokinetic parameters

Liao WH, Liu XR, Su YX et al. · 2026 Nov 06
Study Type: Retrospective two-centre diagnostic modelling study (n=133), with training, internal and external validation cohorts. Retrospective design is inferred from "consecutive patients"; the abstract does not state it explicitly.
Key Question: Can DCE-MRI pharmacokinetic parameters (Ktrans, Kep, Ve) distinguish tumour from cephalic peritumoral oesophageal tissue at 1–5 cm from the margin, indicating microvascular heterogeneity in ESCC?
Key Findings:
  • Parameters differed between tumour and peritumoral tissue at 1, 2 and 3 cm, but not between 3, 4 and 5 cm, so these were pooled (PT3–5).
  • A combined Ve_CV + Kep_mean model discriminated tumour vs PT2 (AUC 0.830/0.917/0.818) and tumour vs PT3–5 (AUC 0.921/0.845/0.857) across training, internal and external cohorts.
  • Ve_CV alone performed best for tumour vs PT1 (AUC 0.716/0.872/0.787).
Clinical Relevance: DCE-MRI may eventually help define the extent of tumour-related microvascular change beyond the visible margin, which could inform target volume delineation or surgical margins, though no direct clinical application is demonstrated.
Limitations: Small sample with modest validation cohorts, no histopathological correlation of peritumoral microvascular change, and no assessment of clinical outcomes or utility.
